raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old previously healthy male was admitted to our medical unit with a history of fever of 5-day duration. He had high-grade fever associated with generalized aches and frontal headache. He denied any respiratory or urinary symptoms. He mentioned that he had not passed faeces for the last three days but had developed nonbloody diarrhoea on the day of admission without any vomiting or abdominal pain. He denied any recent travel, but he had been eating from various food outlets for the past 2 weeks during his after-school cricket practice sessions.
On examination, he was not ill looking despite his temperature of 40 C. There were no pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, and skin rashes. Cardiovascular and respiratory examination was normal. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, nontender abdomen with a 3 cm nontender hepatomegaly and a 2 cm splenomegaly. His blood test showed a haemoglobin count of 14.8 g/dl, a white cell count of 2.8 x 109/l (neutrophils 79% and lymphocytes 14%), and a platelet count of 97 x 109/l. Dengue NS1 antigen and IgM against dengue virus detected by a commercial kit (Standard Diagnostics, Inc., Germany) were negative. C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated more than 250 mg/dl in two subsequent samples. His liver function tests were normal except elevated liver transaminases (ALT 145 U/l and AST 118 U/l; ALT/AST normal range 8-40 U/L). An ultrasound scan of the abdomen confirmed mild hepatosplenomegaly. On days 2 and 3 of his admission, he continued to have high fever spikes, diarrhoea, and persistent thrombocytopenia with a high CRP.
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily was commenced. After 48 hours, the patients' clinical condition had not improved and the high fever spikes continued. After antibiotic susceptibility test results, his antibiotic was changed to imipenem 1 g 8 hourly. He showed clinical improvement after 48 hours, but the diarrhoea and fever settled only around the 10th day of treatment. Imipenem was continued for a total duration of 14 days. His platelet count, liver transaminases, and CRP returned to normal. A repeat blood and faeces culture performed on discharge was negative for Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, generalized body aches, and frontal headache, followed by same-day onset of non-bloody diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high-grade fever associated with generalized aches and frontal headache for 5 days. After 3 days without passing stool, he developed non-bloody watery diarrhea on the day of admission without nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. No recent travel, but reported frequent consumption of food from outside street/food outlets over the preceding 2 weeks after school cricket practice.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, generalized body aches, frontal headache, 3-day constipation followed by non-bloody diarrhea. Pertinent negatives: no vomiting, abdominal pain, respiratory symptoms, or urinary symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient did not appear toxic despite a temperature of 40 °C, with no pallor, icterus, lymphadenopathy, or skin rash. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, non-tender abdomen with a 3 cm non-tender hepatomegaly and a 2 cm splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 14.8 g/dL, leukopenia with WBC 2.8 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 79%, lymphocytes 14%), thrombocytopenia with platelets 97 x 10^9/L, markedly elevated CRP >250 mg/dL on two serial samples, and elevated transaminases with ALT 145 U/L and AST 118 U/L (normal range: 8-40 U/L; other LFT parameters normal). Dengue NS1 antigen and dengue IgM antibody tests were negative. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed mild hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Blood/fecal culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing identified extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) / ceftriaxone-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi susceptible to carbapenems (imipenem).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Typhoid fever caused by cephalosporin-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, confirmed by culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Dengue fever was ruled out via negative NS1 antigen and IgM serology. Initial empirical therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 48 hours failed to resolve his high fever spikes, diarrhea, or thrombocytopenia. Guided by susceptibility results, therapy was switched to intravenous imipenem 1 g every 8 hours for 14 days; clinical improvement began within 48 hours, fever and diarrhea completely resolved by day 10 of treatment, and platelets, transaminases, and CRP normalized. Repeat blood and stool cultures at discharge were negative for S. Typhi.
